subject: Chemistry
title: Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry
summary: Chemistry counts particles in moles: 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number), and its mass in grams equals the molar mass.
Laws of chemical combination (conservation of mass, definite proportions, multiple proportions, Gay-Lussac's law, Avogadro's law) led to Dalton's atomic theory.
A balanced equation is a recipe in moles. The reactant that runs out first is the limiting reagent and decides how much product forms.
Concentration can be expressed as mass %, mole fraction, molarity (mol/L, changes with temperature) or molality (mol/kg of solvent, temperature-independent).

formulas.name: Mole concept
formulas.formula: n = mass/M = N/Nₐ = V(gas at STP)/22.4 L
formulas.when: Converting between mass, particles and gas volume.
formulas.mistake: 22.4 L is only for a gas at STP (273 K, 1 atm) — never for liquids or solids.

formulas.name: Atomic mass unit
formulas.formula: 1 amu (u) = 1/12 × mass of one ¹²C atom = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g

formulas.name: Percentage composition
formulas.formula: % of element = (mass of element in 1 mol / molar mass) × 100

formulas.name: Empirical and molecular formula
formulas.formula: molecular formula = n × empirical formula;  n = molar mass / empirical formula mass
formulas.note: Convert % to moles, divide by the smallest, then round to whole numbers (multiply if you get .5 or .33).

formulas.name: Limiting reagent
formulas.formula: compare (moles available ÷ coefficient) for each reactant — the smallest is limiting
formulas.when: Product amount when reactants are not in the exact ratio.
formulas.mistake: Don't compare masses — compare moles divided by stoichiometric coefficients.

formulas.name: Mass percent
formulas.formula: w/w % = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100;   ppm = (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 10⁶
formulas.when: Concentration by mass; ppm for very dilute solutions (pollutants in water, air).

formulas.name: Molarity
formulas.formula: M = moles of solute / volume of solution (L)
formulas.note: Molarity changes with temperature because volume does.

formulas.name: Molality
formulas.formula: m = moles of solute / mass of solvent (kg)
formulas.mistake: Use the mass of SOLVENT, not of solution.

formulas.name: Dilution and mixing
formulas.formula: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂;  mixing: M = (M₁V₁ + M₂V₂)/(V₁ + V₂)

formulas.name: Neutralisation (acid–base)
formulas.formula: n₁ × M₁ × V₁ (acid, n = basicity) = n₂ × M₂ × V₂ (base, n = acidity)

examples.title: Counting atoms
examples.problem: How many atoms are present in 4.4 g of CO₂?
examples.solution: n = 4.4/44 = 0.1 mol; each molecule has 3 atoms → 0.3 × 6.022 × 10²³ ≈ 1.81 × 10²³ atoms.

examples.title: Limiting reagent
examples.problem: 10 g of H₂ reacts with 64 g of O₂. Mass of water formed?
examples.solution: H₂ = 5 mol, O₂ = 2 mol. 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O: O₂ needs 4 mol H₂, so O₂ is limiting → 4 mol H₂O = 72 g (1 mol H₂ left).

examples.title: Molarity
examples.problem: 0.5 mol of NaCl is dissolved to make 250 mL of solution. Molarity?

examples.title: Molality from mass %
examples.problem: A solution is 20% NaOH by mass. Molality?
examples.solution: 100 g solution: 20 g NaOH = 0.5 mol in 80 g water. m = 0.5/0.080 = 6.25 m.

examples.title: Mole fraction
examples.problem: 46 g of ethanol is mixed with 54 g of water. Mole fraction of ethanol?

examples.title: Titration volume
examples.problem: Volume of 0.1 M H₂SO₄ to neutralise 50 mL of 0.2 M NaOH?

examples.title: Molarity of commercial acid
examples.problem: H₂SO₄ is 49% by mass with density 1.5 g/mL. Molarity?

topics.title: Matter and its classification
topics.explain: Matter is a pure substance (element or compound) or a mixture (homogeneous like air or salt solution; heterogeneous like sand in water). Compounds have fixed composition; mixtures don't.

topics.title: Laws of chemical combination
topics.explain: Conservation of mass (Lavoisier); definite proportions (Proust) — a compound always has the same elements in the same mass ratio; multiple proportions (Dalton) — masses of one element combining with a fixed mass of another are in small whole-number ratios (e.g. CO and CO₂); Gay-Lussac — gases combine in simple volume ratios; Avogadro — equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules.

topics.title: Dalton's atomic theory
topics.explain: Matter is made of indivisible atoms; atoms of one element are identical; compounds form by atoms combining in fixed ratios; reactions rearrange atoms. Later work showed atoms are divisible and isotopes exist.

topics.title: Measurement and significant figures
topics.explain: Use SI units. Keep answers to the right number of significant figures: × ÷ → fewest significant figures; + − → fewest decimal places. Scientific notation (N × 10ⁿ) makes this clear.

topics.title: Stoichiometry in practice
topics.explain: Balance the equation first. Convert everything to moles, use the mole ratio from the equation, then convert back to mass or volume. Percentage yield = (actual/theoretical) × 100.

topics.title: Choosing a concentration unit
topics.explain: Molarity is easy to use in the lab but changes with temperature; molality and mole fraction don't, so they are used for colligative properties. ppm = (mass of solute/mass of solution) × 10⁶ for very dilute solutions.
